questions.q: A 3-day-old neonate presents with fever, irritability, and a faint orange-red macular rash on the face that rapidly spreads to the neck and axillae. Within 36 hours, large flaccid bullae form and rupture, leaving denuded areas with varnish-like crusting. Notably, the oral mucosa appears completely normal. Which protein is being enzymatically cleaved by the causative staphylococcal toxins?
opts: Desmoglein-3 (Dsg3)
Desmoglein-1 (Dsg1)
E-cadherin
Bullous pemphigoid antigen (BP180)
questions.exp: SSSS is caused by staphylococcal exfoliative toxins (ETA and ETB) that specifically cleave Desmoglein-1 (Dsg1), a cadherin-type adhesion glycoprotein located in superficial epidermal desmosomes. The cleavage occurs at the level of the stratum granulosum, creating subepidermal separation. Dsg3 is preserved on mucosal surfaces, which explains why oral mucosa remains spared despite extensive cutaneous involvement.
questions.🏰 Palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a STAIRCASE of Desmosomes—toxins SHRED the first step (Dsg1 at the GRANULAR layer), but leave the basement intact; meanwhile, MOUTH domes remain DSG3-protected like vault doors.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with a geographic port-wine stain on the left lower limb, progressive limb length discrepancy, and varicose veins noted since age 2. Duplex ultrasound confirms slow-flow venous and lymphatic malformations without arterial shunting. Which genetic mechanism underlies this clinical presentation?
opts: Germline RASA1 mutation inherited in autosomal dominant pattern
Somatic postzygotic gain-of-function PIK3CA mutation causing PI3K/AKT/mTOR hyperactivation
High-flow arteriovenous fistulae from VEGF-A upregulation
Supernumerary ring chromosome 21 with triplosensitive dosage imbalance
questions.exp: Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome is driven by somatic postzygotic gain-of-function PIK3CA mutations encoding the catalytic p110α subunit of PI3K, leading to constitutive hyperactivation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway—the master regulator of growth, proliferation, and angiogenesis. This somatic (not germline) mutation, restricted to a localized lesional clone, explains the sporadic inheritance and non-heritable nature of KTS.

questions.q: A 3-month-old Asian neonate is found to have extensive, dark, rapidly progressive Mongolian spots involving the trunk, shoulders, extremities, and anterior chest—far beyond the typical lumbosacral distribution. Which of the following inborn errors of metabolism is the neonate at highest risk for and warrants urgent metabolic screening?
opts: Acute intermittent porphyria and variegate porphyria
Lysosomal storage diseases including GM1 gangliosidosis type 1, Hurler's disease, and Hunter's disease
Mitochondrial cytopathies and oxidative phosphorylation disorders
Peroxisomal disorders such as Zellweger syndrome and adrenoleukodystrophy
questions.exp: Extensive, dark, and progressive Mongolian spots extending beyond the classic sacral region serve as a major cutaneous red flag for underlying lysosomal storage diseases (LSDs), including GM1 gangliosidosis type 1, Hurler's disease (MPS I), Hunter's disease (MPS II), Niemann-Pick disease, mannosidosis, and mucolipidosis II. The pathophysiology involves accumulation of glycosaminoglycans and lipids that alter dermal pigmentation patterns.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: A HUGE BLUE STAIN spreads across the ENTIRE CASTLE like a SPILL OF TOXIC LYSOSOMAL WASTE—when Mongolian spots go EXTENSIVE and PROGRESSIVE, think LYSOSOMAL STORAGE DISEASES (LSDs) lurking beneath.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with ivory-white papules and nodules (2–8 mm) coalescing into a reticular 'pebbly' pattern on his back and scapulae. He has extensive Mongolian blue spots, generalized hirsutism, and coarse facial features. Genetic testing reveals mutations in the IDS gene causing iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency. Which of the following features would DISTINGUISH this condition from MPS Type I?
opts: Presence of severe corneal clouding
Absence of corneal clouding and presence of pathognomonic ivory papules in a pebbly pattern
Autosomal recessive inheritance pattern
Deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase enzyme
questions.exp:
MPS Type II (Hunter Syndrome) is the only X-linked recessive mucopolysaccharidosis and is characterized by the pathognomonic ivory-white papules/nodules forming a 'pebbly' pattern on the back and scapulae. Crucially, it LACKS corneal clouding, which is a key distinguishing feature from MPS Type I (Hurler Syndrome), which does present with severe corneal clouding. The IDS gene mutation causing iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency is specific to MPS II.
🏰 Palace: Picture a HUNTER (X-linked male) with an IVORY CASTLE roof (pebbly papules) on his BACK—but his EYES are CRYSTAL CLEAR (no corneal clouding). MPS I wears CLOUDY GOGGLES instead.

questions.q: A 650-gram male infant born at 24 weeks' gestation presents on day 3 of life with a severe 'burn-like' exfoliative erythroderma with weeping erosions and intertriginous maceration. Blood cultures and cerebrospinal fluid analysis are being sent. Which of the following statements BEST explains why this extremely low birth weight premature infant is at risk for invasive/systemic candidiasis rather than benign cutaneous disease?
opts: Candida albicans preferentially produces hyphal forms in premature infants due to higher amniotic fluid pH
Very-low-birth-weight premature neonates lack adequate barrier function and systemic immunity, permitting deep visceral dissemination beyond superficial epithelial layers
The stratum corneum is thickened in premature infants, forcing fungal elements to invade deeper epidermal layers
Premature infants have elevated IL-17 levels that paradoxically promote systemic dissemination
questions.exp: Very-low-birth-weight premature neonates (<1000 g, <27 weeks) have immature skin barriers and developing immune defenses, allowing Candida to disseminate systemically into lungs, liver, spleen, blood, and CNS rather than remaining confined to stratum corneum. This invasive form presents as 'burn-like' exfoliative erythroderma with mortality rates approaching 40%, mandating urgent parenteral antifungal therapy.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with severe blistering sunburns after minimal sun exposure, progressive neurological decline, and short stature. Genetic testing reveals mutations in the XPA gene. Which of the following best describes the primary molecular defect in this patient's condition?
opts: Defective translesion synthesis polymerase causing inability to replicate across UV-induced DNA lesions
Loss of XPA protein responsible for DNA damage verification in the nucleotide excision repair pathway
Mutations in ERCC3 gene encoding a helicase component of the TFIIH transcription/repair complex
Autoimmune attack on melanocytes mediated by HLA-associated pathogenic antibodies
questions.exp: XP-A results from autosomal recessive mutations in the XPA gene on chromosome 9q22.23, which encodes the XPA protein critical for DNA damage verification in NER. This is the most common subtype in Japan and presents with severe clinical features including exaggerated photosensitivity and neurodegeneration (De Sanctis-Cacchione Syndrome when complete loss-of-function occurs). Xeroderma pigmentosum is fundamentally a disorder of genomic instability due to defective DNA repair enzymes, not an autoimmune condition.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why a patient with generalized Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (Ritter's disease) presents with striking periorificial crusting and radial fissuring around the mouth and nose, yet the intraoral mucosa remains completely unaffected?
opts: The exfoliative toxins preferentially target epidermal desmoglein-1 while mucosal surfaces express desmoglein-3, which is resistant to staphylococcal proteases
Saliva contains natural antibodies that neutralize the exfoliative toxins at the mucosal border
The oral mucosa has a thicker keratinized layer that prevents toxin penetration
Staphylococcus aureus cannot produce toxins in the presence of oral anaerobic flora
questions.exp: The exfoliative toxins are glutamate-specific serine proteases that exclusively cleave Desmoglein-1 (Dsg1), which is the primary adhesion molecule in superficial epidermis. In contrast, mucosal surfaces predominantly rely on Desmoglein-3 (Dsg3) for cellular adhesion, which remains completely unaffected by staphylococcal exofolative toxins. This explains the pathognomonic pattern of periorificial involvement with mucosal sparing.
questions.🏰 Palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine MOUTH as a FORTRESS with DSG3 SHIELDS—toxins only cut DSG1 SWORDS, so the mucosal MOAT remains unbreached while the skin-WALLS crumble around the GATE.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with poorly defined, round-to-oval hypopigmented macules and patches on his cheeks covered with fine powdery scale. The lesions fail to tan upon sun exposure. Histologically, the epidermis shows mild spongiosis with lymphocyte exocytosis, hyperkeratosis, and parakeratosis. What is the primary pathogenic mechanism underlying the hypopigmentation in pityriasis alba?
opts: Loss of melanocytes due to autoimmune destruction mediated by pathogenic autoantibodies
Disruption of melanosome transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes by low-grade eczematous dermatitis, with possible direct tyrosinase inhibition by dicarboxylic acids or low serum copper
Increased epidermal turnover leading to accelerated shedding of pigmented keratinocytes
Defective synthesis of tyrosinase gene expression secondary to HLA-B27 haplotype association
questions.exp: Pityriasis alba is fundamentally a low-grade localized eczema resulting in post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, not an autoimmune disorder. The pathogenic mechanism involves physical disruption of melanosome transfer by eczematous inflammation, combined with potential direct inhibition of tyrosinase by Malassezia-derived dicarboxylic acids or depleted serum copper—distinguishing it from vitiligo and other immune-mediated depigmentary disorders.

questions.q: Which of the following findings would distinguish Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome from Parkes-Weber syndrome in a child presenting with a port-wine stain and limb hypertrophy?
opts: Presence of a geographic capillary malformation
Progressive soft-tissue and bony overgrowth of the affected limb
Absolute absence of fast-flow arteriovenous fistulae or arterial shunts on imaging
Onset of varicose veins by age 3 years
questions.exp: The critical diagnostic distinction between KTS and Parkes-Weber syndrome is that KTS is strictly slow-flow (capillary-lymphatic-venous malformations) with mandatory absence of fast-flow arterial shunts. Parkes-Weber shares the phenotype of capillary stain and limb hypertrophy but is defined by underlying high-flow arteriovenous fistulae. The complete absence of arterial fast-flow is therefore a mandatory criterion for KTS diagnosis.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy with loose anagen syndrome experiences easy hair shedding with minor friction. Which anatomical structure's faulty keratinization is responsible for the impaired hair anchoring in this condition?
opts: The outer root sheath (ORS) of the telogen hair follicle
The inner root sheath (IRS) of the anagen hair follicle
The dermal papilla and connective tissue sheath
The sebaceous gland ductal epithelium
questions.exp: Loose anagen syndrome results from a structural defect strictly localized to the inner root sheath (IRS) of the anagen hair follicle. Faulty or premature keratinization of the IRS leads to impaired adhesion between the hair shaft cuticle and the companion layer, causing poor anchorage and easy mechanical dislodgement with normal daily activities.

questions.q: A 2-year-old from Singapore develops fulminant hand-foot-and-mouth disease with mucocutaneous lesions followed rapidly by brainstem encephalitis, aseptic meningitis, and acute flaccid paralysis. He deteriorates with pulmonary edema and hemorrhage. Which viral serotype is most likely responsible?
opts: Coxsackievirus A16
Coxsackievirus A6
Enterovirus 71
Echovirus 5
questions.exp: Enterovirus 71 (EV-A71) is the causative agent of severe, neurologic hand-foot-and-mouth disease with tropism for the central nervous system and cardiopulmonary tissues, causing brainstem encephalitis, encephalomyelitis, aseptic meningitis, acute flaccid paralysis, and potentially fatal pulmonary edema. Since the late 1990s, massive severe epidemics have occurred in the Asia-Pacific region, making EV71 the critical differential diagnosis in geographic regions like Singapore, particularly in children under 5 years.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: At the ASIA-PACIFIC castle gates, a DEADLY VIRUS (EV71 written as '7-1' on a tombstone) invades the BRAINSTEM TOWER, paralyzing the guards and flooding the cardiopulmonary chambers with blood—imagine children under 5 collapsing as the virus breaches the BLOOD-BRAIN gates in Singapore's plague year.

questions.q: A 10-year-old boy with a strong family history of hidradenitis suppurativa presents with severe follicular lesions, pilonidal sinuses, and unusual involvement of his chest, back, and ears—atypical sites for typical flexural disease. Which clinical phenotype and genetic factor best account for his early-onset, severe presentation?
opts: Axillary-mammary subtype with heterozygous HLA-B27 mutations
Follicular subtype with high copy number β-defensin cluster mutations (DEFB4/DEFB103)
Prepubertal acne variant with isolated DEFB4 haploinsufficiency
Mixed phenotype with acquired nicastrin deficiency from environmental triggers
questions.exp: Early-onset juvenile hidradenitis suppurativa with severe disease, strong family history, and atypical widespread distribution (ears, chest, back, legs) is characteristic of the follicular phenotype. High copy numbers of the β-defensin cluster genes (DEFB4 and DEFB103) on chromosome 8p23.1 are associated with a more severe clinical phenotype. This genetic susceptibility, combined with the follicular subtype's predilection for early onset and greater disease severity, explains his presentation.

questions.q: A 9-year-old girl presents with recurrent painful nodules and sinus tracts in her axillae and inguinal folds. Genetic testing reveals a loss-of-function mutation in PSEN1. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of her condition?
opts: Primary apocrine gland dysfunction with secondary follicular involvement
Defective gamma-secretase leading to impaired Notch signaling and unopposed TLR4-mediated inflammation
Classic autoimmune disease driven by circulating autoantibodies against follicular antigens
Excessive sebaceous gland proliferation with keratin-filled cyst formation
questions.exp: Juvenile hidradenitis suppurativa is an autoinflammatory disorder, not autoimmune. Loss-of-function mutations in gamma-secretase complex subunits (including PSEN1) impair Notch signaling, which normally suppresses TLR4-mediated pro-inflammatory responses. This unchecked innate immune activation drives IL-23/Th17 pathway activation and elevated TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-17. The primary pathology is keratinous occlusion of the follicular infundibulum, not apocrine gland disease.

questions.q: A skin biopsy is performed on a child with suspected hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia. Which histological finding is most specific and diagnostic for this condition?
opts: Inflammatory infiltrate of CD8+ T cells attacking the basal layer of epidermis
Total absence or severe sparsity of eccrine sweat glands and ducts within the dermis with pathognomonic 'bar code' appearance in hair shafts
Deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone
Hyperkeratosis with acanthosis and increased melanin in the stratum basale
questions.exp: Hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is a developmental/genetic disorder, not an autoimmune or inflammatory condition. The pathognomonic histological finding is total absence or severe sparsity of eccrine sweat glands and ducts within the dermis, combined with characteristic 'bar code' appearance (parallel dark bands of various lengths) visible on microscopic analysis of hair shafts. This reflects the fundamental failure of ectodermal appendage morphogenesis due to EDA/NF-κB pathway mutations.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with painful oral ulcers on the tongue and buccal mucosa, followed by characteristic vesicles on his palms and soles. The vesicles are elliptical and aligned parallel to skin lines. Skin biopsy shows intraepidermal vesicles with vacuolar degeneration but NO viral inclusion bodies or multinucleated giant cells. What is the most likely causative agent?
opts: Herpes simplex virus type 1
Coxsackievirus A16
Varicella-zoster virus
Enterovirus 71
questions.exp: Classic hand-foot-and-mouth disease is most commonly caused by Coxsackievirus A16. The clinical presentation of painful oral enanthem followed by football-shaped vesicles on palms/soles, combined with the absence of viral inclusion bodies and multinucleated giant cells on histology, definitively excludes HSV and VZV (which would show these inclusion bodies). Enterovirus 71 presents with similar cutaneous features but is associated with severe neurological complications and CNS tropism.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture CVA16 as a COZY CAMP-FIRE in the castle courtyard—the cheerful flames ('A16') cast football-shaped shadows (the characteristic vesicles) on the PALMS and SOLES, while painful sores sizzle safely WITHOUT the scary inclusion body 'monsters' lurking inside.

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate presents with generalized erythroderma, superficial blistering, and erosions that resemble epidermolysis bullosa. By 3 months of age, the blistering resolves and is replaced by thick, cobblestone-like hyperkeratosis in the flexures with a characteristic pungent odor. Histopathology shows epidermolytic hyperkeratosis with vacuolar degeneration of suprabasal layers and dense keratin clumps. Which genetic mutation is most likely responsible?
opts: SPINK5 gene mutation
KRT1 and KRT10 gene mutations
ALOX12B and ALOXE3 gene mutations
TGM1 gene mutation
questions.exp:
Epidermolytic ichthyosis (Bullous Congenital Ichthyosiform Erythroderma) is caused by mutations in KRT1 and KRT10 genes encoding keratin intermediate filaments. The pathognomonic histologic finding of epidermolytic hyperkeratosis with suprabasal cytolysis and keratin clumping is diagnostic. The progression from neonatal blistering to flexural hyperkeratosis is characteristic of this autosomal dominant condition.
🏰 Palace: Picture a KNIGHT (KRT) in a medieval castle's FLEXURE CORRIDORS, surrounded by CLUMPY KERATIN COBBLESTONES and blisters that eventually harden into thick armor—the transformation from soft blistering to corrugated hyperkeratosis.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child presents with shiny, flat-topped purple papules on the flexural aspects of the wrists and ankles. Which immunological mechanism is primarily responsible for the tissue damage in this presentation of lichen planus?
opts: Circulating IgG and IgA autoantibodies against basal keratinocytes
CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes and CD56+ NK cells directly attacking basal keratinocytes at the dermo-epidermal junction
Complement-mediated destruction via classical pathway activation
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation triggering basophil infiltration
questions.exp: Lichen planus is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune disorder, not a humoral antibody-driven disease. CD56+ NK cells expressing CXCR-3 and releasing IFN-γ and TNF-α recruit CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes that directly target basal keratinocytes at the DEJ. Direct immunofluorescence is negative or shows only non-specific fibrinogen/IgM as secondary phenomena.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a castle's BASEMENT WALL (basal layer) being ATTACKED by EIGHT-LEGGED SPIDERS (CD8+ T-cells) and NATURAL KNIGHT GUARDIANS (CD56+ NK cells) firing arrows of INTERFERON (IFN-γ) and TNF missiles—no ANTIBODY ARCHERS (IgG/IgA) on the ramparts!

questions.q: According to the Mulliken–Glowacki/ISSVA classification paradigm, which of the following best distinguishes vascular malformations from vascular tumours in terms of clinical behaviour?
opts: Vascular malformations present at birth, lack a proliferative phase, and persist lifelong without regression
Vascular malformations show rapid postnatal growth followed by spontaneous involution over years
Vascular tumours are present at birth as subtle lesions and grow proportionally with the child
Vascular tumours are dysplastic vessels lined by quiescent endothelium with normal cellular turnover
questions.exp: Vascular malformations are present at birth, lack a proliferative phase, grow strictly in proportion to the child, and persist for life without regression. By contrast, vascular tumours (like infantile haemangioma) are typically absent or subtle at birth, show rapid postnatal growth driven by endothelial hyperplasia (GLUT1-positive), and eventually involute. The clinical timeline and growth kinetics are diametrically opposite.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 2] ISSVA Classification and Capillary Malformations

questions.q: A 2-day-old Black neonate presents with a poorly circumscribed, grayish-blue macular patch measuring 8 cm in diameter over the lumbosacral region and buttocks. The parents ask why the lesion appears blue despite the presence of melanin. Which optical phenomenon best explains this clinical appearance?
opts: Rayleigh scattering of longer wavelengths by superficial epidermal melanin
Tyndall effect causing selective scattering of shorter blue light wavelengths by deep dermal melanin
Mie scattering of all visible light by dermal collagen fibers
Absorption of blue light by hemoglobin in dermal blood vessels
questions.exp: The characteristic bluish-gray hue of classic Mongolian spots results from the Tyndall effect, wherein shorter blue light wavelengths are preferentially scattered back to the observer's eye by melanin granules located in the deep reticular dermis. This optical illusion occurs because deeper dermal melanin cannot absorb shorter wavelengths as efficiently as longer wavelengths.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: A BLUE KNIGHT stands in the DEEP CASTLE DUNGEON holding a prism—shorter BLUE rays bounce back to his eyes while longer RED rays vanish into the stone (Tyndall effect in deep dermis = blue appearance).

questions.q: A 3-month-old infant presents with a bright red macule on the cheek that was faint at birth but has remained stable in size relative to body growth. On dermoscopy, the lesion blanches completely with pressure. Which immunohistochemical marker would you expect to be NEGATIVE in this lesion?
opts: GLUT1
CD31
Factor VIII
CD34
questions.exp: Vascular malformations are structural embryonic developmental errors with quiescent, flat endothelium and normal cellular turnover, making them universally GLUT1-negative. GLUT1 positivity is the hallmark of vascular tumours (e.g., infantile haemangioma), not malformations. CD31, Factor VIII, and CD34 are panendothelial markers present in all vascular lesions.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 2] ISSVA Classification and Capillary Malformations

questions.q: A 2-day-old full-term neonate presents with an acute onset of widespread erythematous macules on the trunk and extremities, notably sparing the oral cavity and diaper area. The lesions rapidly progressed to vesicles and pustules within 48 hours. Maternal history reveals placement of an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) 6 months ago. Which immune pattern recognition receptor, when stimulated by fungal β-glucan, is most critical for triggering appropriate Th17 cell differentiation in defense against this infection?
opts: Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)
Dectin-1
Pattern recognition receptor 5 (PRR5)
Complement receptor 1 (CR1)
questions.exp: Dectin-1 is the key pattern recognition receptor on macrophages and keratinocytes that binds fungal β-glucan and, via CARD9 signaling, drives IL-17 production and Th17 differentiation—essential for mucocutaneous candida immunity. The clinical presentation of widespread cutaneous candidiasis sparing oral and diaper areas at 2 days of life is classic congenital cutaneous candidiasis in a full-term infant with a maternal IUCD as a risk factor.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the pathogenesis of lysosomal storage diseases (LSDs) with cutaneous manifestations is CORRECT?
opts: LSDs are autoimmune disorders mediated by pathogenic antibodies against dermal autoantigens and show strong HLA associations
LSDs result from mutations in genes encoding lysosomal acid hydrolases, transport proteins, or enzymatic cofactors, leading to macromolecular accumulation in lysosomes
Routine autoimmune serological testing is essential for diagnosis of all LSDs
The primary cellular targets in cutaneous LSDs are epidermal keratinocytes and melanocytes, not dermal fibroblasts or histiocytes
questions.exp:
LSDs are primary inherited genetic metabolic disorders caused by mutations in genes encoding lysosomal enzymes or transport proteins, resulting in catastrophic accumulation of undegraded macromolecules within lysosomes of dermal cells (predominantly macrophages/histiocytes, fibroblasts, and vascular endothelial cells). They are NOT autoimmune conditions, have NO specific pathogenic autoantigens or antibodies, and routine autoimmune testing is non-applicable.
🏰 Palace: Imagine a LYSOSOMAL TRASH BIN (enzyme defect) overflowing with GARBAGE (macromolecules) in a DERMAL MANSION (fibroblasts/histiocytes), while AUTOIMMUNE POLICE (antibodies) stand confused outside—they have NO job here.

questions.q: A 16-year-old girl presents with widespread hypopigmented patches exceeding 2 cm in diameter affecting her trunk, arms, and legs—not limited to the face. Which variant of pityriasis alba is this, and what is the characteristic demographic feature of this presentation?
opts: Classic pityriasis alba with atypical distribution; primarily affects young boys
Extensive (generalized) pityriasis alba; primarily affects teenagers and young adults with female preponderance
Pigmenting pityriasis alba; shows paradoxical hyperpigmentation with blue coloration
Pityriasis streptogenes variant; associated with recent streptococcal infection
questions.exp: The extensive variant of pityriasis alba is distinguished from classic childhood pityriasis alba by its widespread distribution beyond the face, larger lesion size (>2 cm), and different epidemiologic pattern. This variant predominantly affects teenagers and young adults with a marked female preponderance, whereas classic PA favors young children with facial involvement.

questions.q: A 3-week-old female neonate presents with linear, punctate cribriform atrophy of the skin with underlying fat herniation. Genetic testing reveals a loss-of-function mutation in the PORCN gene on Xp11.23. Which of the following best explains why approximately 90% of affected individuals with this condition are female?
opts: Females have two X chromosomes, providing a protective gene dosage effect
The hemizygous male genotype is typically lethal in utero; surviving males require somatic mosaicism or Klinefelter syndrome
Female hormones provide resistance to Wnt signaling pathway disruption
X-linked recessive inheritance requires two mutated alleles, which is rare in males
questions.exp: Goltz Syndrome (Focal Dermal Hypoplasia) is X-linked dominant with loss-of-function PORCN mutations. A complete hemizygous mutation in 46,XY males is embryonic lethal; only ~10% of affected patients are male, and these survive via somatic mosaicism or Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY). Females survive through random X-inactivation (lyonization), creating functional mosaicism.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a MALE EMBRYO being struck dead by a LIGHTNING BOLT labeled PORCN at the castle gates, while FEMALE TWINS dodge it by randomly turning their X-shields on and off—only the BALANCED females survive to adulthood.

questions.q: A 2-year-old girl with Goltz Syndrome presents with bilateral linear streaks of skin atrophy distributed asymmetrically across her trunk and limbs. A dermatologist notes the lesions follow a specific anatomical pattern. Which embryological principle explains this characteristic distribution pattern?
opts: The lesions follow dermatome distribution corresponding to spinal nerve root levels
Random X-chromosome inactivation creates functional mosaicism producing lesions along the lines of Blaschko
The lesions represent areas of secondary infection and inflammation following primary viral exposure
Gravitational effects cause fat herniation to occur preferentially in dependent skin regions
questions.exp: In Goltz Syndrome, the cutaneous lesions in females follow the lines of Blaschko due to random X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization) during early embryogenesis. This creates a functional mosaic of normal and defective dermal cells that migrate during development, producing the characteristic linear, punctate distribution pattern rather than random or inflammatory distribution.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine the CASTLE WALLS being painted by two rival artists (NORMAL X vs MUTANT X) who randomly take turns with their brushes—resulting in ZEBRA-STRIPED BLASCHKO LINES running vertically down the fortress instead of symmetrical stripes.

questions.q: A 9-year-old boy from the Indian subcontinent develops purple, polygonal, pruritic papules on his wrists that show Wickham striae under magnification. The lesions exhibit new linear eruptions along scratch marks. Which eponymous sign describes this linear phenomenon, and what is the peak age of childhood lichen planus onset?
opts: Auspitz sign; peak age 2–4 years
Koebner phenomenon (isomorphic response); peak age 8–12 years
Nikolsky sign; peak age 5–7 years
Darier sign; peak age 12–15 years
questions.exp: The Koebner phenomenon (isomorphic response) is the characteristic feature where new lichen planus lesions arise in lines of physical trauma or scratch marks. The peak age of childhood lichen planus onset is 8–12 years, and the condition is notably more common in Pacific Indians and the Indian subcontinent (up to 20% of cases).
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine KOEBNER the knight scratching the castle walls (8-12 YEAR OLD drawbridge)—each SCRATCH LINE becomes a new PURPLE PAPULE FORTRESS, especially in the INDIAN SUBCONTINENT KINGDOM where this disease RULES (20% prevalence)!

questions.q: A 4-year-old girl presents with diffusely sparse, dull hair that has never grown long despite normal grooming. Parents report the hair is unruly and 'never needs cutting.' Which genetic mutation is most commonly associated with this presentation of loose anagen syndrome?
opts: Heterozygous missense mutation (E337K) in the K6HF keratin gene (KRT75)
Homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the FLG gene
Heterozygous mutation in the SHOC2 gene on chromosome 10q25
X-linked recessive mutation in the AR gene
questions.exp: Type A (Classic/Unruly) loose anagen syndrome is characterized by diffusely sparse, unruly hair that does not grow long, and the primary genetic defect is a heterozygous missense mutation (E337K) in the K6HF keratin gene (also known as KRT75), which disrupts normal keratinization of the inner root sheath. The SHOC2 mutation is specifically associated with syndromic LAS presenting with Noonan-like features, not isolated Type A disease.

questions.q: A term neonate is born encased in a shiny, taut, collodion-like membrane covering most of the body. After 2 weeks, this membrane sheds, revealing persistent generalized erythroderma with fine, white, feathery scales. Associated findings include ectropion, eclabium, and palmoplantar keratoderma. Histopathology shows psoriasiform acanthosis and orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis without keratin clumping. What is the inheritance pattern of this condition?
opts: Autosomal dominant with 50% spontaneous mutations
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
Mitochondrial inheritance
questions.exp:
Congenital Ichthyosiform Erythroderma (Non-bullous form) presents with a collodion membrane at birth and has autosomal recessive inheritance with an incidence of 1 in 100,000–200,000. It is caused by mutations in genes of the ARCI spectrum including ALOX12B, ALOXE3, NIPAL4, PNPLA1, CERS3, and TGM1, affecting lipid processing in the stratum corneum.
🏰 Palace: Imagine RECESSIVE TWINS (AR inheritance) born in a castle WRAPPED IN SHINY COLLODION PARCHMENT, which peels away to reveal FEATHERY SCALES—the collodion baby hallmark of AR ichthyosis.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with recurrent unexplained fevers, sparse scalp hair, and conical-shaped upper incisor teeth. His mother is unaffected but has patchy areas of reduced sweating on her forearms following linear patterns. Genetic testing confirms an EDA1 mutation. Which of the following best explains the mother's clinical presentation?
opts: She is a homozygous carrier with full manifestation of X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia
She demonstrates mosaicism due to X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization) with alternating bands of normal and absent sweating
She has autosomal recessive hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with incomplete penetrance
She carries a protective modifier gene that prevents disease expression in heterozygous females
questions.exp: Heterozygous females with XLHED exhibit mosaicism following the lines of Blaschko due to random X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization), resulting in alternating bands of normal and abnormal eccrine sweat gland function and whorled areas of sparse hair. This creates the characteristic patchy distribution seen in carriers, distinguishing them from fully affected males who have global hypohidrosis.

questions.q: Which UV-induced DNA photoproducts are unable to be repaired in patients with nucleotide excision repair (NER) defects such as XP-A through XP-G?
opts: Only thymine dimers; pyrimidine-pyrimidone photoproducts are repaired by alternative mechanisms
Cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and pyrimidine (6-4) pyrimidone photoproducts
Purine-pyrimidine crosslinks and 8-oxoguanine lesions exclusively
Spontaneous depurination sites and interstrand crosslinks induced by non-solar radiation
questions.exp: The hallmark DNA damage in XP results from inability to repair two critical UV-induced photoproducts: cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs) and pyrimidine (6-4) pyrimidone photoproducts. These lesions accumulate catastrophically in patients with NER-deficient XP complementation groups (XP-A through XP-G), driving premature genomic mutation accumulation and early-onset carcinogenesis.
